summary: A vision-language agent calibrates superconducting transmon chips end-to-end by reading measurement plots and maintaining a structured notebook, specializing itself to one persistent drifting device via gradient-free online adaptation of an interpretable device note without weight updates. On hard-tier chips under budget pressure, six iterations raised worst-case CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.787; a single accepted note raised it to 0.913 on its paired snapshot, and planted-fault studies confirm the note diagnoses hardware defects truth-free while raising the failure floor.
motivation: Calibrating a transmon chip is a sequential decision problem under noise, drift, and finite budget where expert judgment must weigh ambiguous plots and stale beliefs. Real hardware provides no ground truth for backpropagation and requires auditable, per-device strategies without impractical weight fine-tuning.
method: The work co-designs three artifacts: a physics-grounded environment with circuit-quantized truth (scqubits), LTI flux distortion with FIR predistortion, six independently ablatable wall-time-scaled drift channels, mid-scan drift, and gate leakage; a multimodal calibration agent that calls tools, reads rendered plots, maintains a notebook with evidence records and stale-parameter flags, and submits parameters; and a reflector that grows a human-readable device note from truth-free anomaly signatures, admitted by a paired-snapshot accept gate that runs incumbent and challenger on identical frozen snapshots to isolate strategy improvement from device drift.
result: On one hard-tier chip (tight 16/22 call budget), the first accepted note raised measured CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.913 on the same frozen snapshot; over six iterations worst-case CZ rose to 0.787 with variance reduction, reproducing at four-qubit scale. Planted-defect studies show the note diagnoses a dead coupler ($g \times 0.15$) truth-free, with language absent from healthy controls; FIR predistortion achieves 15% better residual RMS than single-pole fitting; and the rendered plot alone recovers $+0.16$ parameter coverage over scalar-only baselines, eliminating catastrophic zero-coverage failures.
